quiz.stem:
A 24-year-old nursing student in Sydney has hepatitis B serology as part of her occupational screening. Results: HBsAg negative, anti-HBc negative, anti-HBs 120 mIU/mL.

What is the correct interpretation?
quiz.explanation:
**Anti-HBs alone** (with negative HBsAg and negative anti-HBc) indicates immunity from **vaccination**. The hepatitis B vaccine contains only surface antigen, so vaccinated people make anti-HBs but never anti-HBc.

Past natural infection would show **anti-HBc positive** plus anti-HBs. Acute or chronic infection would show HBsAg positive. An anti-HBs level of **10 mIU/mL or more** is considered protective, so she meets healthcare worker requirements.

**Principle:** core antibody means the person has met the virus; surface antibody alone means the vaccine.
whyWrong: Chronic infection requires HBsAg positivity for more than 6 months.
Acute infection shows HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc.
Past infection would show anti-HBc as well as anti-HBs.
She has protective anti-HBs levels.

quiz.stem:
A 38-year-old man who injected drugs in his twenties sees a GP in Melbourne. HCV antibody is positive and HCV RNA is detectable. ALT is 78 U/L. APRI score and FibroScan show no cirrhosis. HBV and HIV tests are negative. He takes no regular medications and is keen to be treated.

What is the most appropriate management?
options: Refer to a hepatologist for pegylated interferon and ribavirin
GP-prescribed oral pangenotypic direct-acting antiviral therapy, then check HCV RNA 12 weeks after completion
Monitor LFTs annually and treat only if cirrhosis develops
quiz.explanation:
He has **chronic hepatitis C** (antibody and RNA positive) without cirrhosis. In Australia, **DAAs are PBS-listed without disease-stage restriction** and **GPs can prescribe them**. A pangenotypic regimen (for example sofosbuvir-velpatasvir for 12 weeks or glecaprevir-pibrentasvir for 8 weeks) cures over 95%.

Cure is confirmed by **SVR12**: undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks after finishing. Because cure does not give immunity, harm reduction and retesting if at risk are important.

Interferon is obsolete. Waiting for cirrhosis is no longer appropriate. There is no HCV vaccine. Non-invasive fibrosis assessment has replaced biopsy.
whyWrong: Interferon-based therapy is obsolete.
Treatment is recommended for everyone with chronic HCV regardless of fibrosis stage.
There is no hepatitis C vaccine.
Non-invasive fibrosis testing has replaced routine biopsy.
quiz.ausPearl: Since March 2016, Australia has provided HCV DAAs on the PBS to all adults with chronic HCV, including people who currently inject drugs and prisoners.

quiz.stem:
A 46-year-old man born in China has known chronic hepatitis B diagnosed 10 years ago. He has not had follow-up for 5 years. He feels well. ALT is normal, HBeAg negative, HBV DNA is low. Liver ultrasound 5 years ago showed no cirrhosis. There is no family history of liver cancer.

Which is the most appropriate ongoing plan?
options: Discharge from follow-up as he is an inactive carrier
Lifelong monitoring of ALT and HBV DNA plus 6-monthly liver ultrasound for HCC surveillance
quiz.explanation:
Chronic hepatitis B needs **lifelong monitoring** because the disease can move from an inactive phase back into immune activity. ALT and HBV DNA are checked regularly (typically every 6 to 12 months), with fibrosis assessment.

He also belongs to a **higher-risk group for HCC** (Asian man over 40), so he needs **6-monthly liver ultrasound**, with or without AFP, even without cirrhosis, because HBV can cause HCC in a non-cirrhotic liver.

Antiviral therapy is not currently indicated with normal ALT and low viral load, but would be if he entered an immune active phase, developed cirrhosis, or needed immunosuppression.
whyWrong: Chronic HBV needs lifelong monitoring; 'inactive' can reactivate.
Antivirals are not indicated with normal ALT, low DNA and no cirrhosis.
LFTs alone miss HCC and viral changes.
Non-invasive monitoring has replaced routine biopsy.
